assignment: When people ask for advice, they sometimes talk to more than one person. Explain why seeking multiple opinions can help someone make a better choice. Use specific details and examples in your response.
essay_1:
Last spring my cousin Danielle had to decide if she should take a job at a hospital two states away or stay at the clinic where she had worked for four years. She asked her mom first, and her mom told her to stay. If Danielle had stopped there, she would have had an answer, but it would have been a weak one, because it came from one person. She went on to ask three more people before she picked. I think her story shows why you should ask more than one person before you make a big choice.

The first reason is that every person only sees part of the situation. Danielle's mom thought about how far away the new city was and how Danielle would not know anybody there. Her supervisor at the clinic told her there was no room to move up where she was, and that the hospital would train her in things the clinic did not have. A woman she knew who had moved for work a few years before talked about the cost. She said Danielle would have to pay a deposit on an apartment, more for car insurance, and plane tickets to come home for holidays. None of these people were wrong. Each one just knew about a different piece, but one piece alone would have been a problem, since Danielle needed every piece to see the whole thing.

The second reason is that people mix what they want into what they tell you, and most of the time they do not even notice. Danielle's mom did think staying was the smarter plan, but she was also worried about her daughter living six hours away. If you only hear one opinion, you can not tell which part is facts and which part is what the person wants. When you hear from a few people, you can see where one of them is different from the rest. Danielle noticed that her mom was the only one who kept talking about her being alone. That let her think about it as one thing on the list and not the whole list.

The third reason is that when you compare what people say, you find out what the real question is. If everybody says the same thing, you can pretty much count on it. All four people Danielle asked said the hospital would do more for her career, so she did not have to keep thinking about that part. The part they did not agree on was if moving was worth leaving her family and paying all those bills. That showed her what she still had to figure out by herself. It is kind of like when somebody goes to a second doctor. If both doctors say to get the same surgery, the person can go ahead with it. If the doctors say different things, the person knows to ask more questions first.

Some people say that asking a lot of people just mixes you up. I get that, because a person could keep asking forever so they never have to decide. But that is a problem with asking too many people, not a reason to ask only one. You should ask a few people who know about the subject. Also, getting advice is not the same as doing what you are told. Danielle did not count votes. She listened to everybody and then she picked for herself, so the choice was still hers.

In the end Danielle took the hospital job. She also asked to start a little later so she could put away some pay for the move, and that idea came from the woman who had moved before. She has been there eight months now, and she just started the training her supervisor told her about. She says it is not easy being that far from home, but she does not think she made a mistake. One talk with one person would not have gotten her to that plan. It took four, and that is why I think people should ask more than one person for advice.
essay_2:
Last spring my cousin Danielle had a big decision to make. She could take a job at a hospital two states away, or she could stay at the clinic where she worked for four years. The first person she asked was her mom and her mom said to stay. If Danielle stopped there she would of had her answer, but I don't think it would of been a good one. She asked three more people after that and her decision came out a lot better. I think asking a few people for advice is better then asking just one person.

My first reason is that one person only knows part of the story. Danielle's mom was thinking about how far away the new city was and how lonely Danielle could get there. Her boss at the clinic told her something different. He said there was no way for her to move up at the clinic and that the hospital would teach her things the clinic never could. He didn't even have a reason to want her to leave, he would have to find somebody new, so I think that says a lot. Then she asked a friend who moved for a job a few years ago. Her friend told her about stuff she never thought about, like paying a security deposit and how car insurance costs more there and how much it costs to fly home for the holidays. None of them were wrong. They each knew a different part, and Danielle needed all of the parts before she could see the whole thing.

My second reason is that people put their own feelings in their advice. A lot of the time they don't even know they are doing it. Danielle's mom really did think staying was the smart thing to do. But she also didn't want her daughter living six hours away from her. If you only ask one person, you can't tell what part is facts and what part is just what that person wants. When you ask a few people you can tell. Danielle noticed that her mom was the only one who said being lonely was the biggest problem. Being lonely still mattered, but now she could think about it in a fair way and not like it was the only thing.

My third reason is that when you compare what people say, you find out what you really have to decide. If everybody says the same thing then it is probably right. All four people said the hospital was better for her career, so Danielle didn't have to worry about that part anymore. The part they didn't agree on was if moving was worth it for the rest of her life, like her family and friends. So that was the part she had to figure out by herself. It is kind of like getting a second opinion from a doctor. If two doctors both say you need the same surgery, you feel better about getting it. If they say different things, then you know you should ask more questions first.

Some people say that asking too many people will just confuse you. I think that can be true sometimes. There are people who keep asking and asking so they never have to pick. But that doesn't mean you should only ask one person. It means you should ask a normal amount of people, and they should be people who know something about it. Also getting advice is not the same thing as doing what everybody tells you. Danielle didn't count up votes. She listened to all of them and then she picked for herself. That made it her own decision. It wouldn't of been her own if she just did what her mom said.

In the end Danielle took the hospital job. She asked if she could start later so she could save up money for the move, and that was her friend's idea. She has been there eight months now and she just started the training her boss told her about. One conversation could not of gotten her to that plan. It took four of them. That is why I think you should always ask more than one person when you have a big choice to make.
